bridges.mechanism: Higher rates of missile, artillery and drone strikes near coasts and on naval/port targets produce more direct attacks, mines and collateral damage to shipping, increasing the frequency and severity of hostile incidents on sea lanes.
Kinetic strikes that damage export infrastructure (ports, loading terminals, storage tanks, pipelines) or render berths unusable directly reduce the volume of crude that can be loaded and exported.

A rapid spike in high-intensity kinetic operations in Ukraine forces NATO/US to reassign maritime and air assets to Europe for deterrence and logistics, reducing the pool of forces available for forward presence in the Iran-proxies theater.

High-intensity, large-scale missile and strike operations in Ukraine normalize massed long-range fires and damage thresholds, prompting North Korea to increase readiness, threat-posturing and pre-emptive signaling that raise escalation pressure on the Korean peninsula.

Spikes in intense kinetic operations increase perceived demand for ISR, autonomy and defense technology, prompting private and strategic investors to reallocate capital into AI firms and funds positioned to supply those capabilities.

Sabotage, mines laid by small craft, and cyber intrusions against traffic-control/navigation aids or port systems can force temporary closures or routing restrictions at narrow straits and approaches, lowering accessibility for commercial traffic.

A rise in cross‑border cyber intrusions, AI‑enabled influence and sabotage linked to the conflict prompts legislatures and regulators to tighten controls on AI security, export, and certification rules to reduce abuse vectors.

Stronger perceived unity among allied states enables coordinated economic measures and joint interdiction/logistics (e.g., sanctions enforcement, naval escorts/interdictions) that constrain a belligerent's ability to export crude.

A visible weakening of coalition unity over the Ukraine war (policy splits, delayed commitments) leads partner states to reduce or pause regional rotations and burden-sharing, producing a measurable drop in foreign force posture in the Middle East theater.

Stronger and more visible cohesion among US/ROK/Japan deterrent postures reduces opportunities for Moscow and Beijing to expand political and operational leverage over Pyongyang, lowering external patron influence on DPRK decision-making.

Tighter security alignment among the US and partners drives coordinated procurement, certification and network‑trusting arrangements that favor a small set of vetted Western cloud and HPC providers, increasing market concentration of high‑end compute.

Sustained increases in Western military aid to Ukraine prompt Russia and its partners to accelerate transfers of kamikaze drones, anti-ship missiles and exportable targeting gear to Iran and allied militias, which materially raise proxy capacity to execute maritime attacks.

Sustained increases in Western military aid to Ukraine raise Russian incentives to offset losses and sanction-pressure by accelerating bilateral arms transfers and permissive brokering to partners like North Korea, raising the volume of weapons and delivery systems entering DPRK networks.

Large, sustained military aid packages include procurement contracts, R&D funding and classified data-sharing with defense contractors and national labs, which accelerates development and fielding of higher‑performance AI models relevant to both military and commercial deployments.

Escalating kinetic and non-kinetic hostilities raise perceived operational and insurance risk and force longer routings or escorts, which increases charter costs and insurance premiums embedded in freight rates.

As Iranian-proxy fighting intensifies, Iran and its proxies accelerate urgent procurement of rockets and missile components, prompting increased clandestine arms transfers from alternative suppliers including North Korea and raising the overall volume of weapons flows tied to the crisis.

Escalation by Iran-linked proxies correlates with accelerated transfers of drones, precision munitions and technical assistance from Iran (and its networks) to Russia, enabling an increase in the tempo and destructiveness of kinetic strikes in Ukraine.

Rising kinetic and asymmetric hostilities raise geopolitical and operational risk perceptions among investors and institutional LPs, causing a pullback or reallocation of financing away from cross-border and high-risk AI ventures linked to the affected region.
An increased rate of hostile actions against vessels directly raises the frequency and severity of incidents experienced by commercial shipping, thereby increasing measured maritime security risk.

A sharp rise in maritime attacks forces Western governments to reallocate naval assets, munitions stocks and political bandwidth to secure merchant shipping and partners in the Middle East, producing measurable delays and down‑prioritisation of weapons deliveries and financing destined for Ukraine.

Increased attacks on commercial and military shipping directly delay, damage, or divert shipments of high-end GPUs, networking gear and other compute-critical hardware, reducing the short-term accessible training and inference capacity for affected operators.

When actors exert effective control or denial over narrow sea passages they physically restrict passage and impose inspections/interdictions, reducing the passability of those chokepoints for commercial traffic.

A surge in external forces deployed to the Gulf ties U.S. and allied assets and attention to the Middle East, which Pyongyang interprets as reduced U.S. focus/response capacity in East Asia and therefore increases DPRK incentives to pursue missile tests and other escalatory signaling.

Large-scale deployments of Western forces to counter Iran-proxy escalation create intra-alliance friction over burden‑sharing and rules of engagement, producing visible policy divergence and weakening perceived NATO/partner unity on collective deterrence vis‑à‑vis Russia.

A stepped-up presence of external militaries in the Iran-proxy theater generates domestic political pressure and security assessments that prompt governments (especially the US and its allies) to tighten export controls, vetting, and sanctions on dual-use technologies implicated in the theater.
Higher rates of rerouting, delays, seizures and port interruptions directly reduce the volume of crude that can be loaded and shipped on schedule, lowering crude export flows.

Disruption to commercial shipping raises energy and food prices and supply bottlenecks in donor countries and in Ukraine, triggering public unrest and political pressure that erodes government stability and sustained public support for continued involvement in the Ukraine war.

Sustained disruption to commercial maritime traffic disproportionately harms smaller cloud and colo providers with thin inventories, enabling large, vertically integrated providers with diversified supply lines and stockpiles to increase market share for high-end compute.

Higher AI capability accelerates deployment of autonomous maritime drones, improved targeting/decision software and automated ISR that lower thresholds for tactical interdiction and raise the likelihood of misidentification or incidents near chokepoints, increasing hostile encounters affecting commercial shipping.

Rapid improvements in deployable AI (ISR, target recognition, logistics optimization) lower integration time and operational risk for advanced militaries, encouraging increased forward deployments and persistent allied force posture in the theater as deterrence and force-multiplication.

Rises in frontier AI capability accelerate deployment of sensor-fusion, target-recognition and autonomous guidance software in loitering munitions, artillery spotting and strike planning used by combatants, raising the rate and accuracy of kinetic strikes.

An increase in accessible high‑end compute dedicated to allied ISR, targeting analysis and air‑defense simulation shortens detection-to-intercept cycles and strengthens deterrence, reducing the frequency of DPRK cross‑border attacks.

Expanded high-performance compute access allows rapid training and operation of large generative and offensive cyber models (deepfakes, phishing automation, automated vulnerability discovery), which actors deploy to scale cyber intrusions, influence campaigns and small-drone/sabotage targeting in the theatre.

When high‑end compute is concentrated in a small number of compliant providers, those firms (under pressure from export controls and sanctions enforcement) can suspend accounts and block hosted design/coordination services used in illicit procurement and weapons development, constraining the tempo and volume of arms-related transfers into the DPRK network.

Tightened export controls and licensing on AI-enabled targeting, sensor-fusion, and maritime-autonomy technologies restrict proxies' ability to acquire and operate high-precision guidance and autonomous maritime/drone systems, reducing the frequency and effectiveness of attacks on vessels.

Tighter export controls and vetting on AI and dual‑use tech reduce legal channels and increase compliance risk for Chinese intermediaries, diminishing Beijing's ability to supply or broker operationally valuable tech to Pyongyang and thereby lowering external patrons' operational leverage over DPRK decision‑making.

Unilateral tightening of AI export controls or cross-border tech rules by the US/allies produces compliance divergences and friction with partners (commercial and policy), degrading synchronized intelligence-sharing and joint deterrence posture.
Increased cross-border kinetic or missile strikes into or over adjacent seas directly raise the frequency and severity of hostile incidents affecting commercial vessels and sea lanes.

Rising escalation pressure prompts coastal states and naval commanders to impose navigation warnings, temporary restrictions or localized closures around narrow passages, reducing normal passability for commercial shipping.

Rising escalation pressure raises geopolitical risk premiums and uncertainty for cross-border technology ventures, causing international investors and funds to scale back or delay financing for civilian AI companies tied to the region, lowering net capital flows into AI.

Greater external-patron leverage (naval escorts, diplomatic pressure, or targeted restrictions) forces rerouting, longer voyages or imposes operational constraints that translate directly into higher chartering and insurance costs for tanker voyages.

A rise in external patron influence over North Korea heightens policymaker fears of coordinated tech transfer and dual-use proliferation, prompting quicker and broader export controls, licensing restrictions and sanctions on AI-related goods and services.

A surge in weapons and munitions shipments in regional sea lanes leads shipowners and operators to withdraw or refuse employment of tankers for voyages to/through affected ports or zones, shrinking the deployable tanker stock.

Increased shipments from North Korea of anti-ship missiles, cruise missiles, sea-skimming munitions, drones and naval mines directly raise Iranian-proxy strike capability and enable a higher tempo of maritime attacks against military and commercial vessels.
Direct shipments of North Korean artillery, rockets or missile munitions to Russian front-line units increase available stocks and enable higher-tempo, larger-scale barrages and missile strikes.
Weapons and munitions exported by North Korea to Russia constitute an increase in actual military transfers into the Russia–Ukraine theatre, raising measured military aid flows to a combatant.

Increased arms shipments and related parts through regional logistics routes lead to interdictions, targeted sanctions and supply-chain disruptions that interrupt deliveries of high-end chips and leased compute hardware, reducing accessible compute capacity in affected markets.

Sharp reductions in crude export flows prompt consumer states and partners to deploy naval/air assets to protect producers and sea lines of communication, increasing foreign military presence in the region.

A sustained drop in crude export volumes and related export revenues (e.g., from Russian sales disrupted by maritime interdiction or chokepoint closures) reduces government fiscal capacity and subsidies, heightening inflation and social grievances that erode domestic political stability.
When chokepoint accessibility falls (due to mines, interdictions or harassment), local actors can more easily enforce area-denial and thereby consolidate de facto control over the passage.

Physical restriction or temporary closure of key sea passages (e.g., Black Sea approaches or the Turkish Straits) prevents or substantially delays roll-on/roll-off and heavy-equipment shipments to Ukrainian ports, forcing cancellations or long detours that reduce the volume and tempo of maritime military aid.

Improved passage through key maritime chokepoints speeds delivery of advanced chips and servers to training sites, accelerating hardware refresh cycles and enabling higher aggregate AI model training and deployment performance.

A rise in maritime security incidents normalizes and signals capability for hostile actors, lowering operational friction and prompting an increase in the tempo and rate of maritime attacks by Iran-aligned proxies.

A rise in hostile incidents on key sea lanes near the peninsula directly prompts reciprocal naval/military deployments, alerting and hardening actors on all sides and thereby increasing the systemic pressure to escalate.

A rise in attacks or clear threats to commercial shipping near the conflict triggers allied naval escorts, joint patrols, and coordinated diplomatic responses, increasing perceived unity and operational coordination among partners.

A rise in hostile incidents and attacks forces port closures, rerouting and inspection delays that directly slow or prevent delivery of datacenter fuel, replacement parts and accelerator hardware, producing immediate reductions in usable high-performance compute.

A decline in available tanker tonnage forces route juggling, shipment cancellations and longer laytimes, directly raising the rate and severity of commercial shipping disruptions for crude and refined products.

Greater commercial tanker availability enables external patrons to deliver fuel and sanctioned commodity assistance more reliably by sea, which they can condition or time to extract political and operational leverage over North Korea.

A sharp decline in available tanker tonnage for transporting fuel and lubricants to the theatre constrains frontline fuel resupply for vehicles, aircraft and logistics, lowering operational tempo and thereby reducing the overall rate and scale of kinetic strikes.

Greater availability of tanker tonnage eases fuel and bulk-transport bottlenecks, reducing the logistical advantage of the largest, vertically integrated cloud providers and enabling smaller operators to secure resources, thereby lowering compute-market concentration.

Sustained increases in freight and insurance costs raise upfront and operating costs for AI projects and cloud capacity expansion, reducing projected returns and causing investors and corporates to scale back or delay AI financing.

Kinetic strike intensity
nodes.description: The overall rate, scale and destructiveness of direct kinetic attacks (air, missile, artillery, large drones) across the theatre.

nodes.label: Weapon-technology diffusion
nodes.description: The speed and breadth with which weapons designs, delivery systems and enabling technologies spread between actors and proxies.

nodes.label: Hybrid attack activity
nodes.description: The frequency and geographic reach of non-kinetic and ambiguous operations such as cyber intrusions, sabotage, electoral influence and small-drone strikes.

nodes.label: Alliance deterrence cohesion
nodes.description: The perceived unity, policy alignment and credibility of collective defence commitments among security partners.

nodes.label: Force deployment density
nodes.description: The concentration and forward posture of military forces and assets positioned in or near contested regions.

nodes.label: Military aid flows
nodes.description: The volume, tempo and composition of transfers of weapons, equipment, logistics and finance to combatants and partners.

nodes.label: Sanctions pressure
nodes.description: The intensity, scope and enforcement rigor of economic, financial and trade restrictions applied across actors.

nodes.label: Energy trade interdependence
nodes.description: The depth and asymmetry of energy and key commodity trade links that create economic leverage or vulnerability between actors.

nodes.label: Domestic political stability
nodes.description: The resilience or fragility of domestic political systems, including government durability and protest/polarisation dynamics.

nodes.label: Public war support
nodes.description: Aggregate popular support, fatigue or opposition within societies toward continued military engagement and external aid.

nodes.label: Proxy partnership strength
nodes.description: The depth, institutionalisation and resource-exchange capacity of indirect partnerships and proxy networks.

nodes.label: Information operation intensity
nodes.description: The scale, sophistication and reach of coordinated messaging, disinformation and influence campaigns across media channels.

nodes.label: Critical infrastructure vulnerability
nodes.description: The exposure and fragility of civilian and logistical infrastructure (transport, energy, communications) to disruption or attack.

nodes.label: Financial market volatility
nodes.description: Cross-border financial stress measured by asset price swings, capital flight, liquidity squeezes and transaction interruptions.

nodes.label: Arms stockpile
nodes.description: The available inventories of munitions, spare parts and deployable weapons that determine sustainment of military operations.

nodes.label: Nuclear rhetoric intensity
nodes.description: The frequency, escalation and coercive severity of declaratory nuclear or extreme-escala­tion threats and messaging.

Conflict intensity
nodes.description: The overall kinetic and non-kinetic intensity of hostilities in the conflict theater, measured by frequency and scale of attacks and operations.

nodes.label: Maritime attack rate
nodes.description: The rate at which hostile actions (missile, drone, naval interdiction, mines, etc.) are executed against commercial and military vessels in the maritime domain.

nodes.label: Chokepoint control
nodes.description: The degree of effective control or denial over strategic maritime transit points, reflecting control of sea-lanes and access through narrow passages.

nodes.label: Proxy support flow
nodes.description: The volume and frequency of material, financial, intelligence, and advisory support transmitted through indirect channels to armed non-state actors.

nodes.label: Foreign military presence
nodes.description: The aggregate scale and posture of external military forces and assets deployed or operating within the regional theater.

nodes.label: Military logistics resilience
nodes.description: The capacity of combatant forces to sustain operations over time through supply, maintenance, and force generation systems.

nodes.label: Energy infrastructure vulnerability
nodes.description: The susceptibility of energy production, processing, and distribution infrastructure to disruption or attack.

nodes.label: Commercial shipping disruption
nodes.description: The rate and extent of interruptions to commercial maritime traffic including rerouting, delays, and seizures.

nodes.label: Legal and diplomatic pressure
nodes.description: The intensity and frequency of legal actions, diplomatic protests, sanctions, and formal international disputes arising from the conflict.

nodes.label: Regional alliance cohesion
nodes.description: The degree of alignment, coordination, and mutual support among regional security partners and formal/informal coalitions.

nodes.label: Energy price volatility
nodes.description: The fluctuation magnitude and frequency in global and regional energy commodity prices attributable to supply risk perceptions and disruptions.

nodes.label: Shipping insurance costs
nodes.description: The prevailing premium rates and risk surcharges for marine hull and cargo insurance covering routes in and near the conflict zone.

nodes.label: Civilian displacement rate
nodes.description: The flow rate of civilian population movement away from conflict-affected areas due to insecurity and infrastructure damage.

nodes.label: Command-and-control integrity
nodes.description: The functional coherence and survivability of military command, control, communications, and decision-making systems under stress.

nodes.label: Maritime interdiction capability
nodes.description: The operational capacity to interdict, board, inspect, or deny passage to vessels through naval, air, and coastal assets.

AI capability level
nodes.description: The aggregate technical performance and generalization ability of leading AI models and architectures available for deployment.

nodes.label: Compute capacity available
nodes.description: The total accessible high-performance compute (training and inference) across datacenters and leased resources per unit time.

nodes.label: Compute price
nodes.description: The unit cost of procuring high-performance compute (e.g., GPU/TPU-hour) for model training and inference.

nodes.label: Capital flows into AI
nodes.description: The rate and scale of financial investment directed toward AI development, compute financing, and AI-linked instruments.

nodes.label: Financialization of compute
nodes.description: The extent to which compute resources are packaged, traded, insured or otherwise treated as financial assets and instruments.

nodes.label: Compute provider concentration
nodes.description: The market share concentration of a small number of providers in the supply of high-end compute resources.

nodes.label: Corporate safety and governance robustness
nodes.description: The overall strength of organizational structures, processes and resourcing dedicated to AI risk management and governance.

nodes.label: Safety incident rate
nodes.description: The frequency of observable safety, security or misuse events linked to deployed AI systems per unit time.

nodes.label: Rogue agent misuse incidence
nodes.description: The rate at which autonomous or agentic AI behaviours are exploited, go rogue, or cause covert malicious actions.

nodes.label: Regulatory stringency
nodes.description: The strictness and scope of legal and policy constraints applied to AI development, deployment and related markets.

nodes.label: Geopolitical AI rivalry intensity
nodes.description: The intensity of interstate strategic competition and policy friction specifically tied to AI capabilities, supply chains and standards.

nodes.label: Talent mobility rate
nodes.description: The flow rate of skilled AI researchers, engineers and technical talent across firms and national borders.

nodes.label: Cross-border data flow volume
nodes.description: The throughput of training-relevant data moving between jurisdictions and organizations available for model development.

nodes.label: Public trust and fear
nodes.description: The aggregate level of public confidence, concern or fear about AI technologies and their societal impacts.

nodes.label: Media attention intensity
nodes.description: The volume and tempo of news and commentary covering AI developments, incidents and policy debates per unit time.

nodes.label: Investor concentration
nodes.description: The degree to which financial exposures and portfolio weight are concentrated in a small set of AI-exposed assets or firms.

Non-state armed group offensive capability
nodes.description: The aggregate combat power, reach and strike-readiness of non-state armed actors operating in the theatre.

nodes.label: State military defensive capacity
nodes.description: The ability of state-aligned forces to detect, deter and absorb attacks and to defend territory and critical infrastructure.

nodes.label: Cross-border attack rate
nodes.description: The frequency at which kinetic or remote-attack operations cross international boundaries per unit time.

nodes.label: Maritime chokepoint control
nodes.description: The degree to which any actor or coalition exerts effective control or denial over strategic sea lanes and straits.

nodes.label: External support flow to local actors
nodes.description: The rate of transfer of materiel, funding, intelligence and advisory support from outside actors to local forces.

nodes.label: Regional naval presence density
nodes.description: The concentration of naval and maritime security assets operating in and near key sea lanes and littoral zones.

nodes.label: Energy infrastructure vulnerability
nodes.description: The susceptibility of energy production, processing and transport assets to disruption or damage from attacks or spillovers.

nodes.label: Shipping reroute rate
nodes.description: The proportion or volume of commercial maritime traffic diverting from primary routes to avoid perceived risks per unit time.

nodes.label: Legal and basing restrictions
nodes.description: The degree of legal, diplomatic and host-state constraints on the use of foreign bases and overflight/operational rights.

nodes.label: Diplomatic engagement intensity
nodes.description: The level and frequency of formal diplomatic interactions, negotiations and crisis-management efforts among relevant actors.

nodes.label: Escalation pressure
nodes.description: The net systemic tendency toward intensification of conflict, reflecting accumulating triggers, grievances and incentives to escalate.

nodes.label: External patron influence
nodes.description: The political and operational leverage that external patrons exert over local actors' strategic decisions and alignments.

nodes.label: Arms flow volume
nodes.description: The quantity and tempo of weapons, munitions and delivery systems entering the conflict environment per unit time.

nodes.label: Global energy price volatility
nodes.description: The short- to medium-term variability in global energy prices that affects economic and political responses to disruptions.

nodes.label: Maritime interdiction rate
nodes.description: The frequency of interdiction, boarding, seizure or attack events against commercial vessels in the region per unit time.

nodes.label: Perception of legality of military actions
nodes.description: The prevailing international and domestic judgments about the legality and legitimacy of military operations and their political acceptability.

Crude production rate
nodes.description: The volumetric rate at which crude oil is extracted and brought to market per unit time across producing regions.

nodes.label: Producer output quota
nodes.description: The aggregate level of officially signaled or coordinated production targets set by major producing groups or coalitions.

nodes.label: Crude export flow
nodes.description: The volume-per-time of crude oil shipments leaving producing regions and entering international trade lanes.

nodes.label: Refined fuel output
nodes.description: The rate at which refineries convert crude into refined products (diesel, gasoline, jet fuel) available for distribution.

nodes.label: Refinery utilization rate
nodes.description: The proportion of refinery processing capacity currently in operation relative to total installed capacity.

nodes.label: Tanker transit capacity
nodes.description: The effective throughput capacity of oil tanker movements through maritime routes and chokepoints per unit time.

nodes.label: Chokepoint accessibility
nodes.description: The degree to which critical maritime passages (e.g., narrow straits) are passable for commercial shipping relative to normal conditions.

nodes.label: Maritime security risk
nodes.description: The frequency and severity of hostile incidents, attacks, or threats affecting commercial shipping on key sea lanes.

nodes.label: Shipping route deviation
nodes.description: The average increase in voyage distance or transit time caused by rerouting away from preferred sea lanes.

nodes.label: Tanker availability
nodes.description: The stock of commercially available tanker tonnage (idle or deployable) ready to transport crude or refined products.

nodes.label: Global oil inventories
nodes.description: The aggregate volumes of crude and refined product stocks held in commercial storage across markets.

nodes.label: Strategic reserve levels
nodes.description: The volumes of publicly held emergency petroleum reserves set aside to be released in response to supply shocks.

nodes.label: Diesel distribution rate
nodes.description: The flow rate at which diesel is moved from refineries and storage into regional wholesale and retail networks (trucking, local depots).

nodes.label: Diesel price level
nodes.description: The prevailing wholesale or retail price of diesel fuel that reflects market clearing conditions.

nodes.label: Shipping freight rates
nodes.description: The cost level for chartering and insuring tanker voyages, including freight, insurance, and risk surcharges.

nodes.label: Market risk premium
nodes.description: The additional price component market participants assign to fuels and freight to compensate for perceived supply disruption risk.

Rising escalation pressure raises geopolitical risk premiums and uncertainty for cross-border technology ventures, causing international investors and funds to scale back or delay financing for civilian AI companies tied to the region, lowering net capital flows into AI.

Greater external-patron leverage (naval escorts, diplomatic pressure, or targeted restrictions) forces rerouting, longer voyages or imposes operational constraints that translate directly into higher chartering and insurance costs for tanker voyages.

A rise in external patron influence over North Korea heightens policymaker fears of coordinated tech transfer and dual-use proliferation, prompting quicker and broader export controls, licensing restrictions and sanctions on AI-related goods and services.

A surge in weapons and munitions shipments in regional sea lanes leads shipowners and operators to withdraw or refuse employment of tankers for voyages to/through affected ports or zones, shrinking the deployable tanker stock.

Weapons and munitions exported by North Korea to Russia constitute an increase in actual military transfers into the Russia–Ukraine theatre, raising measured military aid flows to a combatant.

Increased arms shipments and related parts through regional logistics routes lead to interdictions, targeted sanctions and supply-chain disruptions that interrupt deliveries of high-end chips and leased compute hardware, reducing accessible compute capacity in affected markets.

When chokepoint accessibility falls (due to mines, interdictions or harassment), local actors can more easily enforce area-denial and thereby consolidate de facto control over the passage.

Physical restriction or temporary closure of key sea passages (e.g., Black Sea approaches or the Turkish Straits) prevents or substantially delays roll-on/roll-off and heavy-equipment shipments to Ukrainian ports, forcing cancellations or long detours that reduce the volume and tempo of maritime military aid.

Improved passage through key maritime chokepoints speeds delivery of advanced chips and servers to training sites, accelerating hardware refresh cycles and enabling higher aggregate AI model training and deployment performance.

A rise in maritime security incidents normalizes and signals capability for hostile actors, lowering operational friction and prompting an increase in the tempo and rate of maritime attacks by Iran-aligned proxies.

A rise in hostile incidents on key sea lanes near the peninsula directly prompts reciprocal naval/military deployments, alerting and hardening actors on all sides and thereby increasing the systemic pressure to escalate.

A rise in attacks or clear threats to commercial shipping near the conflict triggers allied naval escorts, joint patrols, and coordinated diplomatic responses, increasing perceived unity and operational coordination among partners.

A rise in hostile incidents and attacks forces port closures, rerouting and inspection delays that directly slow or prevent delivery of datacenter fuel, replacement parts and accelerator hardware, producing immediate reductions in usable high-performance compute.

Greater availability of tanker tonnage eases fuel and bulk-transport bottlenecks, reducing the logistical advantage of the largest, vertically integrated cloud providers and enabling smaller operators to secure resources, thereby lowering compute-market concentration.

Sustained increases in freight and insurance costs raise upfront and operating costs for AI projects and cloud capacity expansion, reducing projected returns and causing investors and corporates to scale back or delay AI financing.
